exercise1.prompt: A global name and a local greeting, printed together from greet()

cases.name: prints the local greeting
cases.describe: the greeting made inside the function

cases.name: prints the global name as well
cases.describe: the name made outside the function

cases.name: greet reads both its own variable and the one outside it
cases.describe: a greet function that uses both greeting and name

exercise1.hint: A function can read a variable made outside it without being handed it. Check that both values reach the print, and that greeting is created inside the function rather than beside it.

exercise2.prompt: increment_counter() raises a global counter, called twice

cases.name: the counter reads 1 and then 2 across the two calls
the counter is defined outside and changed inside
cases.describe: an increment_counter function that works on counter

exercise2.hint: If the second call prints the same number as the first, the function is working on its own copy. Ask which counter the assignment inside the function is creating.

questions.prompt: A variable is created inside a function. What happens if you print it after the function has finished?
choices: It prints the last value it held
questions.explain: A local variable stops existing when the function returns. Outside, the name was never defined at all, so Python says it does not know it.

questions.prompt: What does the global keyword do inside a function?
choices: It creates a new variable that other functions can read
It says that assignments to this name should change the variable outside the function
It imports the variable from another file
questions.explain: Reading a global needs no keyword. global is only needed when you assign to one, because an assignment inside a function otherwise makes a new local of the same name.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true about local variables?
choices: They are created each time the function runs
They disappear when the function finishes
Two functions may each have a local called total without clashing
They can be read from anywhere in the program
questions.explain: Locals live and die with one run of one function, which is exactly why the same name can be reused safely elsewhere. The last option describes a global, not a local.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of code to what it makes.
left: count = 0 at the top of the file
global count then count = 1 inside a function
right: a new local variable that hides the global
a change to the existing global variable
questions.explain: The same line means different things depending on where it sits, and global is what tells Python you meant the outer one.
